summary: A summary index of RFC numbers 1700 through 1799, listing the documents published in that range. It is a reference list, not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents for one hundred of the Internet's notes, so you can find them.

questions: how many rfcs are in the 1700 range
subtitle: A reference guide to Internet standards and protocols from RFCs 1700–1799.

tldr.problem: Tracking the hundred RFCs published in a specific range (1700–1799) is difficult without a guide. The standards track status of many RFCs changes over time.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides an annotated listing of RFCs 1700–1799, with brief descriptions of what each covers and noting which are on the standards track.
tldr.outcome: Engineers can see at a glance what was published during that period and whether an RFC they encounter is on the standards track.

today: RFC 1799 remains an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It is a historical snapshot; for current information about which RFCs are standards, consult the latest Internet Official Protocol Standards document.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 1799 is a reference guide listing every RFC published between number 1700 and 1799—a hundred documents published mostly between February and June 1995. It is not a technical standard itself, but rather a snapshot in time, describing what each RFC covers in one or two sentences.

The author, Mary Kennedy of USC's Information Sciences Institute, produced this as a status report for the IETF. Not all RFCs are standards; some describe experimental protocols, provide information for the community, or chronicle Internet infrastructure decisions. This document helps readers distinguish which RFCs are standards from the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a master list telling you what 100 different Internet guides do, published one after another in 1995.

sections.title: How the List Is Organized
sections.content:
Each entry begins with the RFC number, followed by the author's name, the publication date, and the title. Below that is a plain-language summary of the RFC's purpose in one or two sentences. For RFCs on the standards track—those advancing toward official Internet standards—the document adds the notation [STANDARDS-TRACK] so readers know they are being actively pursued by the standards process.

The list runs in numerical order from RFC 1700 ("Assigned Numbers", a registry of protocol parameters) through RFC 1799 (the document itself). Each description is brief enough to scan quickly but detailed enough to tell whether the RFC covers something relevant to your work.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry shows the number, who wrote it, when, and what it does in a few words. Some have a special mark meaning they are official standards in the works.

sections.title: The Standards Track
sections.content:
The RFC document series includes several categories. Many RFCs in this range are marked [STANDARDS-TRACK], meaning the IETF is pursuing them as potential Internet standards. Others are marked Informational—they convey useful information but make no claims to be standards. A few are marked Experimental for protocols being tested but not yet ready for broad deployment.

The document explains that the status of RFCs can change as they move through the standards process (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Standard), so this list captures only a moment in time. For the current, definitive status of any RFC, readers are directed to consult the latest "Internet Official Protocol Standards" document, which was RFC 1780 at the time RFC 1799 was written.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these guides are being worked on to become official standards, others are just sharing information, and a few are being tested. The list shows which is which.

sections.title: What This Range Covers
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs from 1700 to 1799 cover a wide spectrum of Internet technologies: directory services (LDAP, X.500), email protocols (IMAP4, POP3, MIME encapsulation), routing (BGP-4, OSPF enhancements, RIP-2), network management (MIBs for Token Ring, printers, AppleTalk), and foundational infrastructure like URLs and resource naming.

Some entries reflect active research into the next generation of IP (IPng), with multiple RFCs exploring competing approaches. Others address deployment and operational questions, such as the treatment of Class A subnets, DNS debugging, and telecommunications integration. This range shows the breadth of work the IETF undertook in the mid-1990s.
sections.plainLanguage: These 100 documents cover mail systems, routing, directories, how to name things, and lots of other parts of how the Internet works.
